content.thinking:
This is a descriptive norm correction telling people 76% of Americans trust climate scientists, which should nudge trust upward since people usually underestimate this figure. Based on similar megastudies like the climate intervention tournament, such norm-based nudges tend to produce fairly small effects, maybe 1-3 points on a 100-point scale.

I'm sketching out estimates across the outcome measures: trust around +1.5-2 points, distrust around -1.2, funding perceptions +0.6, policy role +1.0, institutional trust +0.8, belief +0.5, concern +0.6, general and specific policy support around +0.6-0.8, and behavioral measures a modest +0.4, with donation behavior still to estimate.

The correction on trust prevalence (people underestimating ~50% versus actual 76%) resembles consensus-gap studies, which tend to produce modest but real shifts—so I'm nudging trust_post up to around 2.2 and distrust down to -1.3, while noting possible demand effects from telling respondents trust is already high.

content.text: {"reasoning_summary": "This arm is a descriptive-norm / false-consensus correction: respondents first guess how many Americans trust climate scientists (most underestimate, typically guessing ~45-55%), then learn that 76% report at least some trust. Social-proof corrections of this kind produce reliable but modest shifts, and importantly the message conveys nothing new about scientists' actual competence or integrity — only what other people think — so it should move trust less than testimonial or evidence-based arms. The interactive slider plus explicit gap correction adds salience and a mild demand effect, so I expect a small positive effect on the primary trust measure (~1-2 points) with slightly larger movement on the single-item trust question (which is more malleable but anchored on the pre-treatment answer) and a smaller mirror-image drop in distrust. Downstream outcomes (belief, concern, policy, behavior) are anchored, more crystallized, and only indirectly targeted, so I expect attenuated effects under ~1 point, shrinking further for institutional trust (diluted by the federal-government item) and belief (pre-measured, near ceiling for most). parsed_output.reasoning_summary: This arm is a descriptive-norm / false-consensus correction: respondents first guess how many Americans trust climate scientists (most underestimate, typically guessing ~45-55%), then learn that 76% report at least some trust. Social-proof corrections of this kind produce reliable but modest shifts, and importantly the message conveys nothing new about scientists' actual competence or integrity — only what other people think — so it should move trust less than testimonial or evidence-based arms. The interactive slider plus explicit gap correction adds salience and a mild demand effect, so I expect a small positive effect on the primary trust measure (~1-2 points) with slightly larger movement on the single-item trust question (which is more malleable but anchored on the pre-treatment answer) and a smaller mirror-image drop in distrust. Downstream outcomes (belief, concern, policy, behavior) are anchored, more crystallized, and only indirectly targeted, so I expect attenuated effects under ~1 point, shrinking further for institutional trust (diluted by the federal-government item) and belief (pre-measured, near ceiling for most). Incentivized real behaviors (donation, newsletter) should be near zero, with maybe a few cents and half a percentage point at most.
